rows.speaker: bazıları
rows.claim: Some attach the opening lām to a verb in the previous sūra; others prefer supplying an omitted verb here to preserve this sūra’s independence.
rows.anchor: Bunu bazıları sûrenin istiklâline münâfî görerek

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Elephant event cannot be the sole cause of Quraysh’s trade alliances, which already existed from the time of Hāshim and his brothers; the event did strengthen Quraysh’s standing.
rows.anchor: Kureyş’in bu rıhlete ülfeti ve bu bâbda Yemen ve Şam hükûmetleriyle mu‘âhede ve i’tilâfları yalnız fil vak‘asından sonra değil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām is causal, but attaches to the coming command to worship, making ilāf a distinct divine favor to Quraysh rather than the Elephant event’s sole rationale.
rows.anchor: lâm’ın ta‘lîl için olmakla beraber yukarıki sûre mazmûnuna değil, ancak ilerideki فَلْيَعْبُدُوا۟ emrine müte‘allik olmasıyla mümkindir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although a famous grammar rule says a clause after fa cannot govern what precedes it, Qur’anic examples show that this fa does not prevent the proposed attachment.
rows.anchor: Fâ’nın mâba‘di mâkablinde âmil olamayacağına dair meşhur bir nahiv kāidesi var ise de

rows.speaker: İmam Halil ve Sîbeveyh
rows.claim: The grammarians al-Khalīl and Sībawayh explicitly attach the lām to the command فَلْيَعْبُدُوا۟; the language scholars of al-Kashshāf also choose this reading.
rows.anchor: nahiv eimmesinden İmam Halil ve Sîbeveyh bu lâm’ın فَلْيَعْبُدُوا۟’ya müte‘allik olduğunu beyan ve tasrih etmişler

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author explicitly adopts this syntactic reading in his translation.
rows.anchor: biz de mealde bu vechi açık olarak tercih ve ihtiyar eyledik

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address is to the Messenger, who is told to command Quraysh; ilāf means a brought-about and desired increase in their familiarity and alliances, especially noteworthy after the Elephant event.
rows.anchor: Hitab da Resûlullah’a olup Kureyş’e emir, emr-i gāib olduğu için mânanın hâsılı şu olmuş olur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase can explain their becoming accustomed to winter and summer travel, receiving welcome at destinations, or making agreements and treaties with surrounding peoples.
rows.anchor: kışın ve yazın göçe, sefere ülfet ettirildikleri veya daha ziyade ettirilmeleri için

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rihla means a migration or journey; if ilāf is Form IV, rihla is its direct object, while under Form III it is a purpose object with an implied preposition.
rows.anchor: “Rıhlet” mâlum ki göç, sefer demektir. “Îlâf” if‘âlden olduğuna göre “rıhlet” onun mef‘ûl-i bihi

rows.speaker: İbn Abbas
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says Quraysh travelled to Yemen in winter and to Busra in Syria in summer for trade; they also summered in Ṭāʾif and wintered in Mecca.
rows.anchor: İbn Abbas’tan rivayet edildiği üzere Kureyş ticaret için kışın Yemen’e, yazın da Şam tarafına Busra’ya sefer ederlerdi

rows.speaker: Nakkāş
rows.claim: Al-Naqqāsh reports that Quraysh made four journeys; Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects this account.
rows.anchor: Nakkāş tefsirinde dört rıhletleri olduğu zikrolunmuş, İbn Atıyye bu kavlin merdud olduğunu söylemiş

rows.speaker: Bahr
rows.claim: Al-Baḥr says rejection is unwarranted: four brothers of ʿAbd Manāf secured routes to Syria, Abyssinia, Yemen, and Persia, and protected Quraysh merchants using their names.
rows.anchor: ashâb-ı îlâf dört birader idi ki bunlar Abdi Menaf oğullarıdır

rows.speaker: Ezherî
rows.claim: Al-Azharī defines ilāf as protection resembling a safe-conduct or guardianship, called hufāra.
rows.anchor: Ezherî ‘el-îlâf شِبْه الإِْجَازَةِ بِالْخُفَارَةِ yani hufâre[^36] denilen yasakçılıkla koruyuşa[^37] benzer’ demiştir

rows.speaker: Bahr
rows.claim: The four protected destinations do not conflict with the verse’s two seasonal journeys: rihla is generic and can denote one or many journeys.
rows.anchor: ‘Rıhlet’ ism-i cins olarak bir ve daha ziyade sefere de şâmil olabilir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unnamed poet praises the brothers for securing regional treaties, travelling on the ilāf journey, supporting the poor, and welcoming guests; the lines illustrate the broader sense of the verse.
rows.anchor: الآْخِذُونَ الْعَهْدَ مِ نْ آفَاقِهَا وَالرَّاحِلُونَ لِرِحْلَةِ الْإِْيلَاَ فِ

rows.speaker: Kāmûs
rows.claim: The lexicon describes Quraysh as sanctuary residents who travelled safely for provisions while surrounding people were attacked; Hāshim obtained a Syrian safe-conduct and his brothers obtained similar treaties for other regions.
rows.anchor: Kureyş, Harem-i şerîf’in sükkânı idiler, etraflarında halk vurulup çarpılırken onlar erzaklarının celbinde

rows.speaker: Okyanus
rows.claim: Okyanus recounts that Hāshim secured a formal safe-conduct from the Syrian ruler after receiving an audience with Caesar, enabling Quraysh merchants to travel safely.
rows.anchor: İbtidâ Hâşim b. Abdi Menaf Şam melikinden ahd ü eman almıştı

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ilāf carries two related senses: mutual agreement or treaty (Form III), and protection that habituates another to travel (Form IV).
rows.anchor: “îlâf” tâbiri iki haysiyetle iki mâna ifade etmiş oluyor

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word’s two occurrences may signal these two senses, and Ibn ʿĀmir’s reading distinguishes the first as ilāf and second as īlāf; the translation should retain the word to encompass both.
rows.anchor: İbn Âmir kıraati de[^43] birincinin “ilâf”, ikincinin “îlâf” olmasında sarihtir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Trade journeys are the basic referent, though Quraysh’s protection may also have enabled other people’s journeys.
rows.anchor: Bütün bu mânalarda رِحْلَةَ ٱلشِّتَآءِ وَٱلصَّيْفِ’de ticaret seferi mânası esas olmuş oluyor

rows.speaker: Fahr-ı Râzî
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī offers another possible reading: the journeys are other people’s Hajj and ʿUmra trips to Mecca, encouraged by Quraysh’s provision of safety; the wording allows it, but the trade reading is more famous.
rows.anchor: Fahr-ı Râzî’nin ikinci bir kavil olarak zikrettiği vechile bu kış ve yaz rıhletinden murad sâir halkın hac ve umre için Mekke’ye sefer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh’s trade familiarity began before the Elephant event; the event later confirmed and reinforced its benefits because destroying the Kaʿba would have ended Quraysh’s standing and alliances.
rows.anchor: Kureyş’in bu rıhletlere ülfeti fil vak‘asından sonra başlamış değildir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām of purpose can refer to an intended future benefit as well as an already-existing cause, as in saying one spoke to make someone love him.
rows.anchor: Mef‘ûl-i leh mutlaka husûlî olmak lâzım gelmez; illet-i gāiye, fâide-i müterettibe kabîlinden

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The intended mature ilāf is a worldwide alliance promising civilization, safety, and peace, rooted in honoring the sanctuary, the Prophetic mission, and monotheism rather than petty trade alone.
rows.anchor: bütün cihâna karşı ülfet ve i’tilâf ile yüksek bir medeniyet, emn ü âsâyişi taahhüd edecek mütekâmil bir îlâf

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Existing alliances and trade are blessings to thank, while the higher unity sought through them rests on monotheistic worship; the ilāf gift is foregrounded to direct Quraysh to worship.
rows.anchor: husûle gelmiş bulunan îlâfın ve ticaretin de şükrü lâzım gelen bir ni‘met-i rabbâniye

rows.speaker: sâhib-Keşşâf
rows.claim: Al-Kashshāf reasons that even if Quraysh do not count God’s other blessings, they should worship the Lord of the House at least for this gift of ilāf.
rows.anchor: sâhib-Keşşâf’ın beyan ettiği vechile mâna şu olur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh should stop resisting Muhammad’s call and shirk, recognize the truth, and worship only the peerless Lord of the Kaʿba.
rows.anchor: da‘vet-i Muhammediye üzerine serkeşlik etmeyip hakkı tanısınlar, şirk ü isyandan vazgeçsinler

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative pronoun is an attribute of “Lord.”
rows.anchor: {ٱلَّذِىٓ} “Rabb”in sıfatıdır, yani bu Beyt’in o Rabbi ki

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite endings on hunger and fear magnify their severity.
rows.anchor: “cû‘”un ve “havf”ın tenvinleri tefhıym ve tehvîl içindir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation links their nourishment to Abraham’s prayer for provision for his descendants in barren Mecca; Quraysh survived through the fruits supplied there.
rows.anchor: Beyt-i Muharrem’in yanında Mekke ziraatsız bir vâdi olduğu hâlde Hazret-i İbrâhîm’in duası ve Kâbe’nin hurmeti sayesinde

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clearest interpretation is that Abraham’s prayer and the House’s blessing, through the winter and summer trade journeys, protected Quraysh from the hunger naturally expected in that region.
rows.anchor: burada en zâhir olan budur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third view sees a severe famine like Joseph’s years, when people ate carrion and bones and were relieved through the Prophet’s prayer, though Quraysh’s unbelievers remained unbelieving.
rows.anchor: Yûsuf seneleri gibi süren şiddetli kahta işaret olduğunu dahi söylemişlerdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Security includes deliverance from the Elephant army’s threat, safety in the sanctuary while surrounding people were attacked, and safe travel through Quraysh’s alliances.
rows.anchor: bu da ashâb-ı filin def‘edilmiş olan korkusudur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being worthy of the sanctuary requires reforming surrounding injustice, establishing safety, helping the poor, striving in God’s path, and holding sincerely to Islam, as summarized in Sūrat al-ʿAṣr.
rows.anchor: bütün cihâna karşı o etrafın cehalet ve şekāvetini ıslah ve emniyet ü âsâyişini tesis

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūra connects the Elephant sūra backward to the secure city and denial of judgment in al-Tīn, then leads into al-Māʿūn’s question about denying religion.
rows.anchor: buradan yukarıki sûrelere de ircâ‘-ı nazar ettirerek ta Ve’t-Tîni Sûresi’ndeki

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address is to the Prophet and, by implication, anyone able to receive the address; the question is an expression of wonder meant to draw attention.
rows.anchor: Hitab yine Resûlullah’a ve dolayısıyla umûmen hitâba kābiliyeti olanların her birinedir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeing people depend on mutual aid amid hunger, satiety, fear, and safety makes denial of divine recompense astonishing; the question exposes deniers’ character and warns believers against it.
rows.anchor: Hak teâlâ’nın cezâ ve mükâfâtını inkâr edenlerin, dine inanmayanların bulunması taaccüb edilecek bir şey olduğuna tenbih

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dīn here means recompense: God certainly rewards good and punishes evil, so people will encounter what they did; this is a binding truth to affirm and obey.
rows.anchor: Burada da “dîn” en mutlak ve en esaslı mefhûmu olan ceza mânasınadır

rows.speaker: Mukātil
rows.claim: Muqātil reports that the verse was revealed about ʿĀṣ b. Wāʾil al-Sahmī, who denied the Resurrection and acted immorally.
rows.anchor: Mukātil’den bunun Âs b. Vâil-i Sehmî hakkında nâzil olduğu rivayet edilmiş

rows.speaker: Süddî
rows.claim: Al-Suddī reports that it was revealed about al-Walīd b. al-Mughīra.
rows.anchor: Süddî’den Velid b. Mugīre hakkında nâzil olduğu rivayet edilmiş

rows.speaker: Mâverdî
rows.claim: Al-Māwardī transmits that it was revealed about Abū Jahl; a report says he had charge of an orphan, shoved him away when he came destitute asking for his own property, then gave it after the Prophet accompanied him.
rows.anchor: Mâverdî de Ebû Cehil hakkında nâzil olduğunu nakleylemiş

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the orphan account, Quraysh mocked Abū Jahl for giving in; he said two spears appeared beside the Prophet and he feared being struck if he refused.
rows.anchor: velâkin onun sağında solunda birer harbe gördüm, vermezsem vuracak diye korktum

rows.speaker: İbni Abbas
rows.claim: One report from Ibn ʿAbbās says the verse concerns a hypocrite who is both miserly and ostentatious.
rows.anchor: İbni Abbas’tan bir rivayette de hem bahil hem mürâî bir münafık hakkında nazil oldu denilmiştir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūra may have been revealed for one or all of these people, but its ruling applies to everyone like them.
rows.anchor: fakat hükmü onlara mahsus değil, öylelerin hepsine şâmildir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address is to the Prophet: God, in majesty, assuredly bestowed al-Kawthar on him as a gift and favor.
rows.anchor: Yani yâ Muhammed! Emin ol ki Biz Hak Rabbin şân-ı azametimizle sana mahza atıyye ve ihsan olarak kevser verdik

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kawthar derives from abundance and is an intensive adjective or noun meaning an extremely abundant, very great quantity.
rows.anchor: “Kevser” asıl lügatta çokluk demek olan “kesret”ten “cevher” gibi fev‘al vezninde vasıf veya bir isim

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Bedouin woman reportedly described her son as returning with al-Kawthar, meaning that he brought back a great many things.
rows.anchor: “kevserle geldi” dediğini ve bunun

rows.speaker: Kāmûs
rows.claim: The lexicon lists Kawthar as abundance in anything, abundant swirling dust, Islam and prophethood, a school in Ṭāʾif, a generous or noble man, and a river in Paradise from which the rivers of Paradise branch.
rows.anchor: Kāmûs’ta da şöyle der: اَلْكَثِيرُ مِنْ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ “‘Kevser’[^3] her şeyin çoğu

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: From the root, the divine gift’s goodness, and God’s majestic wording, the clearest initial sense is an established, everlasting, limitless abundance of good; exegetes differ on its specific referent.
rows.anchor: bundan ilk anlaşılacak açık mefhum “hayr-ı kesîr”, yani çok pek çok hayır demek olacağında şüphe edilmez

rows.speaker: Resûlullah
rows.claim: An authentic Prophetic report identifies Kawthar as a river, or in some reports a basin, given in Paradise, full of abundant good; the ummah drinks from it at the Resurrection, and some are turned away for what they did after him.
rows.anchor: “Kevser Rabbimin cennette bana verdiği bir nehir -bazı rivayetlerde bir havzdır- ki hayr-ı kesîr ondadır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports from Anas, ʿĀʾisha, Ibn ʿUmar, and Ibn ʿAbbās describe the river’s pearl-domed banks, musk fragrance, greater sweetness than honey and whiteness than milk, vast extent and depth, and its water’s lasting refreshment.
rows.anchor: Enes’ten, Hazret-i Âişe’den, İbn Ömer’den, İbn Abbas’tan müte‘addid hadisler rivayet eylemişlerdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exegetes debate whether the Prophetic pool and the Paradise river are one, whether the pool is the river’s source or outlet, or whether they are distinct; the well-known view places the pool at the Resurrection gathering.
rows.anchor: Bundan dolayı ikisinden[^10] murad bir midir, havz nehrin menba‘ı veya munsabbı gibi midir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some place the pool before the balance and bridge; others place it after these near Paradise’s gate, where the Prophet’s community settles mutual claims, which al-Ālūsī says would be on the transformed earth.
rows.anchor: Bazıları mîzandan ve sırattan evveldir demişler,[^11] diğer bazıları da onlardan sonra cennetin kapısına yakın

rows.speaker: Kādî Zekeriya
rows.claim: Qāḍī Zakariyyā transmits that the Prophet has two basins, one before the bridge and one after it, both called Kawthar.
rows.anchor: Kādî Zekeriya, Peygamber sallallâhu aleyhi [6182] ve sellem Hazretleri’nin biri sırattan evvel

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author reports Qāḍī Zakariyyā’s sounder view as a pool after the bridge and Kawthar in Paradise, with the pool named after the river flowing into it.
rows.anchor: sahihi havzın sırattan sonra ve Kevser’in cennette olduğunu ve onun munsabbı olduğu için

rows.speaker: Âlûsî
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī transmits that the pool itself is not unique to Muhammad; other prophets also have pools for their believing communities, as in the Tirmidhī report that each prophet has one.
rows.anchor: Âlûsî’nin beyânına göre denilmiştir ki: “Bu havz mânasına kevser

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Tirmidhī report says every prophet has a pool and that prophets take pride in which receives more visitors; Muhammad hopes his pool will have the most.
rows.anchor: her peygamberin bir havzı vardır ve hep onlar hangisinin vâridesi

rows.speaker: Tirmizî
rows.claim: Al-Tirmidhī grades the report about the prophets’ pools as hasan gharīb.
rows.anchor: Tirmizî’nin dediği gibi hasen garîbdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Belief in the pools of other prophets is not obligatory, but Ahl al-Sunna regard belief in the Prophet’s pool as obligatory because its reports are famous near mutawātir; some Muʿtazilites deny that obligation.
rows.anchor: Onun için bu havzlara iman ve itikad vâcib değildir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is unanimously obligatory to believe that the Prophet was given Kawthar, but identifying it specifically as a river or pool is not obligatory because other interpretations exist.
rows.anchor: onun bir nehir veya havz olmasına itikad sahih olmakla beraber vâcibdir denemez

rows.speaker: İkrime
rows.claim: ʿIkrima interprets Kawthar as the honor of prophethood, which encompasses the good of both worlds and the happiness of religion and worldly life.
rows.anchor: İkincisi: İkrime’den mervî olduğu üzere şeref-i nübüvvettir

rows.speaker: Fahr-ı Râzî
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī explains prophethood as the second rank after lordship and a pillar of faith: knowing God precedes knowledge of prophethood, which in turn teaches other divine attributes; he sees Muhammad’s mission as the highest form of abundant good.
rows.anchor: Râzî’nin tafsil [6183] ettiği vechile çünkü rubûbiyetten sonra ikinci mertebedir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad’s prophethood is uniquely great: he is the Seal of the Prophets, mentioned first and sent last, commissioned to both kinds, raised first, and his religion will not be abrogated; his virtues exceed enumeration.
rows.anchor: Hâtemü’n-nebiyyîn olan Peygamberimizin[^19] bu yüksek menkabeden hazz u nasîbi hepsinden çoktur

rows.speaker: Fahr-ı Râzî
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says God may have named Muhammad’s prophetic mission Kawthar, citing the covenant that gives Muhammad special precedence among the prophets.
rows.anchor: Râzî burada mâlum olan sâir peygamberlerin mu‘cizâtıyla onun mucizeleri arasında hulâseten bir mukayese yürüttükten sonra demiştir ki

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Interpretations such as the Prophet’s many virtues, Quran, monotheism, Islam, knowledge, wisdom, and the Praised Station all fall within the abundant good of Muhammad’s prophethood and mission.
rows.anchor: kevseri[^22] Peygamber’in fezâil-i kesîresi, ahlâk-ı azîmesi, her hayrı câmi‘olan Kur’an

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some exegetes include the Praised Station among the special gifts of Muhammad’s mission.
rows.anchor: Risâlet-i Muhammediyenin havâssından olan Makām-ı Mahmûd’u da bu meyanda zikretmek iktizâ eder

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third interpretation is the community’s scholars: as heirs of the prophets, they spread knowledge and virtue, share core monotheistic principles while adapting secondary rulings to circumstances, and become a source of mercy like the river.
rows.anchor: Ümmetinin ulemâsıdır, hakikaten ilmen ve ahlâken verese-i enbiyâ olan ulemâ hayr-ı kesîrdir

rows.speaker: Fahr-ı Râzî
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī gives two grounds for scholars’ merit: many followers will accompany each scholar at Judgment, sometimes exceeding a prophet’s following; and scholars who strive from revelation-based texts are rewarded whether correct or mistaken, with ten rewards for the correct and one for the mistaken.
rows.anchor: Bunda fazilet iki vechiledir: Birisi rivayet olunduğu üzere kıyamet günü her peygamber getirilir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who claim the name of ijtihad while following desires instead of sincerely seeking truth do not share this scholarly merit.
rows.anchor: hakkı[^25] aramayıp[^26] da ictihad nâmına hevâ ve isteklerine tâbi‘

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth interpretation is the abundance of the Prophet’s followers; sound reports promise that more than half of Paradise’s people will be from his community.
rows.anchor: ehl-i cennetin nısfından ziyadesi onun ümmetinden olacağı sahih hadislerle va‘d ü tebşir olunmuştur

rows.speaker: Resûlullah
rows.claim: A report portrays other prophets wishing the ablution-bright communities at Judgment were theirs; Muhammad recognizes them as his community, which enters Paradise without reckoning, followed by further large groups.
rows.anchor: Kâbe’nin Rabbi hakkı için bunlar benim ümmetim

rows.speaker: Resûlullah
rows.claim: The Prophet urged marriage and procreation so that his community would grow and he could take pride in it before other communities at the Resurrection, even through an early loss.
rows.anchor: Aleyhissalâtü vesselâm’ın[^29] تـَنَاكَحُوا تـَنَاسَلُوا تَكْثـُرُوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet would rejoice in the great multitude of his followers, including children below the age of religious responsibility; scholars are also included in this meaning.
rows.anchor: Peygamber’in öyle cemm-i gafîr olan ümmetin kesretiyle ne kadar şâd olacağını teemmül etmeli

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fifth interpretation is the Prophet’s abundant descendants, fitting the revelation as a response to enemies who mocked him as cut off after his son died; history fulfilled the promise of a lineage that would not be exhausted.
rows.anchor: Beşincisi: Hazret-i Peygamber’in evlâdlarının kesretidir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third verse makes the descendants interpretation more explicit.
rows.anchor: bu mânayı üçüncü âyetten anlamak daha açık olur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most exegetes prefer the comprehensive lexical meaning abundant good; every proposed worldly or otherworldly gift is included within it.
rows.anchor: müfessirlerin çoğu “hayr-ı kesîr” mânasında ısrar etmişlerdir, çünkü asıl lügaten mefhum olan en şümullü mâna odur

rows.speaker: Mücâhid
rows.claim: Ibn Jarīr and Ibn ʿAsākir transmit the abundant-good interpretation from Mujāhid; it is also famous from Saʿīd b. Jubayr and Ibn ʿAbbās.
rows.anchor: İbn Cerîr ve İbn Asâkir bunu Mücâhid’den rivayet etmiş oldukları gibi

rows.speaker: İbn Abbas
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains Kawthar as the good God gave His Messenger; he includes the Paradise river within that broader good.
rows.anchor: “‘Kevser’, Allah teâlâ’nın ona, yani Resûlüne i‘tâ buyurduğu hayırdır”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Authentic reports about a Paradise river do not invalidate other interpretations: the hadith may specify a perceptible example of the broader abundant-good meaning, preserving the Qur’an’s unrestricted wording.
rows.anchor: cevap, “hayr-ı kesîr” mefhûmunun kat‘iyyet ve şümûlüyle beraber hadislerin bir misâl ile tefsir olması ihtimâlidir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exegetes do not accuse one another of error because all these possibilities fit the verse and supporting evidence; their real disagreement is whether to define Kawthar narrowly as the river or broadly as abundant good.
rows.anchor: söylenen kavillerin hepsi de âyetin mazmûnunda dâhil ve diğer edille ve karâin ile de müeyyed bulunduğu için

rows.speaker: Râgıb
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib records both interpretations: a Paradise river from which the rivers branch, and a great good God gave His Prophet; he also notes the word for a generous man and the verb for something becoming abundant.
rows.anchor: Râgıb Müfredât’ında bu iki mânayı tesbit ederek şöyle der

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For a believer contemplating the unseen through religious intuition, the hadith’s image of a heavenly river is deeper and more evocative; for rational reflection accessible to everyone, abundant good is clearer and more useful.
rows.anchor: cennette bir nehir olması daha derin ve[^42] daha zevkli, daha mânalıdır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The river symbolism also points to the Prophet’s Miʿrāj, where he was shown it near the Lote Tree and witnessed immense signs; this representation implies the other divine gifts that prepared for it.
rows.anchor: o nehrin kendisine Mi‘râc’da gösterildiği ve onun üzerine Sidre-i Müntehâ ref‘olunarak eser-i azîm müşahede ettirildiği

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The broad abundant-good sense includes Islam, wisdom, the merciful Prophetic mission and Quran, Muhammad’s character and otherworldly gifts, the enduring law, scholars, followers, descendants, Miʿrāj gifts, intercession, and the river.
rows.anchor: nihâyet şefaati, cennetteki nehr-i mahsûsu ilh... hep “hayr-ı kesîr” mefhûmunda dâhil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two readings together move Kawthar from an adjective to a religious proper name for the worldly and otherworldly effusions of Islam and Muhammad’s prophethood.
rows.anchor: “kevser” kelimesi lisân-ı şer‘de vasfiyetten ismiyete naklolunarak dîn-i İslâm ve nübüvvet-i Muhammediyenin dünyevî ve uhrevî füyûzât-ı ledünniyesinin ismi olmuştur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because worldly life is finite and slight beside the Hereafter, God’s abundant gift means an everlasting, inexhaustible gift in the Hereafter, a point the sūra’s ending states explicitly.
rows.anchor: Allah teâlâ’nın kevser buyurduğu atâ ise çok pek çok demek olduğu için geçici dünya metâ‘ve servetinden ibaret olmayıp

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Paradise-river hadith expressly interprets the gift in its otherworldly dimension; this completes the future promise of al-Ḍuḥā 93:5 with the stronger past tense and the name Kawthar.
rows.anchor: istikbal sîgasıyla vaad buyurulmuş olan “atâ” burada daha kuvvetli ve daha kesretli olmak üzere

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The past verb may be either a report of a gift already given or a performative utterance that bestows it now, as in a transfer or contract; both report and performative force apply here.
rows.anchor: doğrusu burada ihbar ile beraber inşâ dahi vardır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A past-tense gift does not imply a finite gift: the object must be understood according to its nature, and the endless future flow of Paradise’s bliss cannot all have been delivered in the present.
rows.anchor: i‘tânın müte‘allakı kendi mâhiyetine göre mülâhaza edilmelidir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say the past tense merely guarantees a future event, like the promise in al-Ḍuḥā; the author finds this contrary to the apparent wording because it explains neither a past report nor a present performative.
rows.anchor: hilâf-ı zâhirdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that past tense signals the gift’s greatness and that its enactment is already an observable, unpostponed fact.
rows.anchor: bunda i‘tânın büyüklüğüne ve icrâsı geri bırakılmayıp emr-i mer’î olduğuna işaret edilmiştir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further explanation sets aside temporal force: the gift is an eternal divine decree, since God’s determination of enrichment, happiness, poverty, or misery is not newly occurring.
rows.anchor: Zaman mânası maksud olmayarak bu i‘tânın[^47] ezelde mukadder bir hükm-i rabbânî olduğunu
